text.p: Visiting world leaders laid wreaths at a mausoleum outside Dhaka on Wednesday as Bangladesh celebrated its 26th anniversary of independence from Pakistan.
The armed forces' bugles played the last post at one minute past midnight to commemorate what is officially described as the "black night" genocide on March 25, 1971.
On that night, the Pakistani army gunned down tens of thousands of people in Dhaka -- the capital of what was then East Pakistan -- trying to thwart an independence movement.
Trains and ferries blew sirens, followed by explosions of firecrackers.
Bangladesh proclaimed independence from Pakistan on March 26, 1971, and was liberated on December 16 after a nine-month war in which it received help from India.

Early on Wednesday, Nelson Mandela of South Africa, Suleyman Demirel of Turkey and Yasser Arafat of the Palestinian Authority flew to Savar, 40 km (25 miles) from Dhaka, to lay wreaths at a mausoleum for those who had been killed in the 1971 war.

They were to return to the capital to join Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whom Arafat on Tuesday called the "daughter of my beloved friend," at the day's main function at the historic Suhrawardy garden.
At this garden on March 7, 1971, Hasina's father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, then chief of Pakistan's largest political party, called for "all-out resistance" against the Pakistani army.
Hasina will receive an "independence torch" that has been carried by war veterans across the country, and light the Shikha Chirantan (eternal flame).
Mujib was killed with most of his family in a 1975 army coup. His daughter took office 21 years later following a general election last June.
